prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A lithography method comprises: providing a substrate with a target region; determining a topology of the substrate within the target region; determining a correcting telecentricity profile based on the topology of the substrate within the target region; providing a radiation beam; and projecting the radiation beam onto the target region of the substrate so as to form an image on the substrate. The radiation beam is such that a net direction of the total radiation received by one or more points in the target region of the substrate is chosen in dependence on the determined correcting telecentricity. The correcting telecentricity profile is such that the net direction of the total radiation received by at least one point in the target region of the substrate is chosen so as to at least partially correct for an overlay error introduced by a curvature of a surface of the substrate at said point.

outputs.L1: A lithography method comprises: providing a substrate having a target region; determining a topology of the substrate within the target region; determining a corrective telecentricity profile based on the topology of the substrate within the target region; providing a radiation beam; and projecting the radiation beam onto the target region of the substrate to form an image thereon. outputs.L2: A lithographic process includes supplying a substrate having a target area and identifying the substrate’s topography within that area. Using the identified topography, a compensating telecentricity profile is established. A beam of radiation is then generated and directed onto the substrate’s target area to produce an image. The beam is configured so that, at one or more locations in the target area, the resultant direction of all radiation incident on each location is selected according to the established compensating telecentricity profile. That profile specifies the resultant radiation direction at least at one location so as to compensate, at least in part, for an overlay error caused by local curvature of the substrate surface at that location.
outputs.L3:
A substrate having a defined target region is provided for lithographic imaging. Before the image is formed, the topology of the substrate within the target region is measured to identify variations in surface height, slope, and curvature. Based on the measured topology, a correcting telecentricity profile is calculated. This profile specifies adjustments to the direction of incident radiation across the target region to compensate for overlay errors that may result from local surface curvature.

A radiation beam is then projected onto the target region to form the desired image on the substrate. During projection, the net radiation direction at one or more points within the target region is adjusted in accordance with the correcting telecentricity profile. By locally modifying the radiation direction, the imaging process at least partially compensates for curvature-induced positional shifts, thereby improving overlay accuracy across the target region.
outputs.L4:
A lithographic exposure method is provided for improving image-placement accuracy on a substrate having a non-planar or locally curved surface. Before or during exposure, topographical data are obtained for a target region of the substrate. The data may represent local height, slope, curvature, or combinations thereof at multiple positions across the region. From the measured topology, a correction profile is calculated that specifies a desired telecentricity adjustment as a function of position. The correction profile is selected to compensate for lateral image displacement that would otherwise occur when projected radiation is incident on a surface that deviates from a nominal image plane.

During exposure, the projection system is controlled in accordance with the correction profile so that the net propagation direction of the radiation at the substrate is locally adjusted. This adjustment may be produced by changing the illumination or projection optics, modifying a pupil distribution, steering one or more optical elements, or applying another suitable directional correction. Different portions of the target region may therefore receive radiation at different effective incidence angles corresponding to the local surface orientation. By accounting for substrate curvature in this manner, the method at least partially suppresses curvature-induced overlay errors, reduces positional mismatch between successive patterned layers, and improves overall placement of the projected image on the substrate.

## The Power of “The”

“The” is one of the smallest yet most important words in the English language. Known as the definite article, it appears before a noun when referring to a particular person, place, object, or idea. For example, “the book” suggests a specific book that the speaker and listener already know about.

Although it contains only three letters, “the” helps make communication clearer and more precise. It distinguishes something specific from something general: “a house” can be any house, while “the house” refers to a particular one.

The word also appears in countless titles, expressions, and everyday sentences. Its frequent use makes it easy to overlook, but without “the,” English would sound less natural and often become more ambiguous. This simple word demonstrates how even the smallest elements of language can have a major impact.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a patent-style independent claim for a lithography method that compensates for wafer-topography-induced overlay errors by adjusting the telecentricity of the projected radiation beam.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe a method for determining substrate topology in a target region and using a correcting telecentricity profile to reduce overlay error caused by local surface curvature.
counterfactuals.output:
A method for compensating curvature-induced overlay error may include:

1. **Map the target-region topography.**  
   Measure the substrate height \(z(x,y)\) at multiple locations in and around the target region using a focus sensor, interferometer, confocal sensor, or other surface-height metrology. Fit or interpolate the measurements to obtain a continuous topology map. Local surface slopes and curvature may be calculated from the first and second spatial derivatives of \(z(x,y)\).

2. **Establish a telecentricity calibration.**  
   Expose or measure calibration features at several known focus or height offsets. From their lateral displacement, determine a telecentricity response profile, for example
   \[
   \mathbf T(x,y)=
   \begin{bmatrix}
   \partial \Delta x/\partial z\\
   \partial \Delta y/\partial z
   \end{bmatrix},
   \]
   which may vary across the exposure field. Higher-order terms may be included if lateral displacement is nonlinear with height or surface slope.

3. **Predict local overlay error.**  
   Reference the measured topology to the exposure or alignment plane to obtain the local height deviation \(\delta z(x,y)\). The telecentricity-induced placement error is then estimated as
   \[
   \Delta\mathbf r_{\mathrm{tel}}(x,y)
   =\mathbf T(x,y)\,\delta z(x,y),
   \]
   optionally augmented by terms dependent on local slope, curvature, scan direction, or projection-system distortion.

4. **Generate a correcting telecentricity profile.**  
   Form a spatial correction map having substantially the opposite displacement:
   \[
   \Delta\mathbf r_{\mathrm{corr}}(x,y)
   =-\Delta\mathbf r_{\mathrm{tel}}(x,y).
   \]
   Filter or regularize the map to remove measurement noise and constrain it to corrections that the exposure system can implement.

5. **Apply the correction during patterning.**  
   Use the correction map to modify local pattern coordinates, reticle or beam position, stage trajectory, scanner timing, projection-optics settings, or another available placement actuator. Focus and leveling may also be adjusted to reduce \(\delta z(x,y)\), with the residual error handled by the lateral correction profile.

6. **Verify and iterate.**  
   Measure overlay after exposure, compare it with the predicted residual, and update the topology model or telecentricity calibration. Repeating this process produces a calibrated feed-forward profile that reduces overlay error associated with local substrate curvature.
